chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ali al-Jarmi from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, and you studied from Abd Allah ibn Muskān from Abū Basīr from Abū Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a person in ihram who threw [a stone at] game and hit its leg, causing it to limp. He said: If the gazelle walked on it and grazed while he was looking at it, there is no penalty upon him. And if the gazelle went on its face (died) while he was raising its leg, he does not know what it did, so upon him is its ransom (fidyah) because he does not know, perhaps it has perished. This does not contradict the two previous narrations because the quarter of the value is only obligatory upon him if he broke its leg or foot and then saw it healed afterwards. And in this narration, it hit it, it limped, then it walked and grazed, and there is no contradiction between them. Because the one whose ruling is this does not incur a specific expiation, but rather gives charity in whatever amount he can.

key_terms.مُحْرِمٍ: Person in ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the penalty for a pilgrim in ihram who injures game but it survives?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Istibsar clarifies the distinction between the fixed penalty of one-quarter of the value (for known injury) and the variable fidyah (for uncertain fate), emphasizing that uncertainty in the animal's survival necessitates charitable compensation rather than a fixed fine. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of resolving apparent contradictions by distinguishing between specific conditions, such as the animal grazing versus its unknown status, thereby ensuring the ruling remains consistent with broader principles of ihram penalties.
